'''David Gawen Champernowne''', {{post-nominals|country=GBR|commas=on|FBA|size=100%}} (9 July 1912 – 19 August 2000)<ref name="telegraph">{{cite news| title=Professor David Champernowne | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/1353993/Professor-David-Champernowne.html | newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] | date=4 September 2000}}</ref><ref name="g"/><ref>Obituaries: ''[[The Times]]'', 25 August 2000, p 23; ''[[The Independent]]'', 26 August 2000, p7.</ref> was an English [[economist]] and [[mathematician]].

== Early life and family ==
Champernowne was the only child of Francis Gawayne Champernowne (1866–1921), [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|M.A. (Oxon.)]], a barrister and [[bursar]] of [[Keble College, Oxford]], and his wife Isabel Mary, daughter of George Rashleigh, of Riseley, [[Horton Kirby]], [[Kent]].<ref>{{cite ODNB| title=Champernowne, David Gawenlocked (1912–2000) | 
first=Frank A. | last=Cowell | doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/74505 | date=4 October 2007 }}</ref> The Champernowne family were landed gentry, of [[Dartington]], [[Devon]]; Francis Gawayne Champernowne was a grandson of Arthur Champernowne (1767–1819), [[Saltash (UK Parliament constituency)#MPs 1640–1832|M.P.]] for [[Saltash]] in 1806, who, born to Rev. Richard Harington, second son of [[Harington baronets|Sir James Harington, 6th Baronet]], had taken his maternal grandfather's name on inheriting his estates.<ref>Burke's Landed Gentry, 14th edition, ed. Alfred T. Butler, 1925, p. 316</ref><ref>The Peerage, Baronetage and Knightage of the British Empire for 1881, The Baronetage and Knightage, Joseph Foster, Nichols and Sons, p. 291</ref>

== Education and career ==
Champernowne was educated at [[Winchester College|Winchester]] and [[King's College, Cambridge]], where he was a contemporary and friend of [[Alan Turing]]. After academic work there and at the [[London School of Economics]], he was drafted into the statistical section of the prime minister's office at the beginning of the [[Second World War]] to supply quantitative information to help [[Winston Churchill]] make decisions; then, in 1941, he moved on to become a programme director in the Ministry of Aircraft Production.

He was a Fellow of [[Nuffield College, Oxford]], Director of the Oxford Institute of Statistics during 1945–1948, and [[Professor]] of Statistical Economics at the [[University of Oxford]] (1948–1959), and Professor of Economics and Statistics (later Emeritus) at the [[University of Cambridge]] (1970–2000).<ref name="telegraph"/><ref name="g"/>

In 1953, he published a model of income distribution that generates the [[Pareto distribution]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Simkin |first1=M.V. |last2=Roychowdhury |first2=V.P. |date=December 2010 |title=Re-inventing Willis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0370157310003339 |journal=Physics Reports |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2010.12.004|arxiv=physics/0601192 |s2cid=88517297 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Champernowne |first=D. G. |date=June 1953 |title=A Model of Income Distribution |url=https://academic.oup.com/ej/article/63/250/318-351/5258723 |journal=The Economic Journal |volume=63 |issue=250 |pages=318–351 |doi=10.2307/2227127|jstor=2227127 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He published work on what is now called the [[Champernowne constant]] in 1933, whilst still an undergraduate at Cambridge.<ref name="telegraph"/><ref name="g"/> In 1948, working with his old college friend [[Alan Turing]], he helped develop one of the first [[chess-playing computer program]]s, ''[[Turochamp]]''.<ref>{{cite journal| title=David Champernowne (1912-2000)|url=http://ilk.uvt.nl/icga/journal/contents/content23-4.htm|journal=[[ICGA Journal]]|volume=23|issue=4|date=December 2000|access-date=11 January 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304041323/http://ilk.uvt.nl/icga/journal/contents/content23-4.htm|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The book for which he is most renowned, synthesising a life's work, ''Economic Inequality and Income Distribution'' ([[Cambridge University Press]]), was published in 1998.<ref name="telegraph"/>

His co-editors at the ''[[Economic Journal]]'' found him to be "modest, quirky and humorous".<ref name="g">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2000/sep/01/guardianobituaries1 | newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|title=David Champernowne: Economist who held chairs at both Oxford and Cambridge|first=Brian|last=Reddaway|date=1 September 2000}}</ref>

== Death ==
Champernowne's grave is at the new church at [[Dartington]] in [[Devon]], built by his family in the 1870s to replace the ancient church at [[Dartington Hall]], the family seat.
